text.p: The Philippine president's wife has begun packing her things, but no-one is sure whether her husband is ready to leave the presidential palace with her.
The country's constitution -- drafted a decade ago to stop dictators like the late Ferdinand Marcos -- stipulates that this is the final year of Fidel Ramos's six-year term.
But a group who want Ramos to run for president again is seeking a change to the rules, triggering a furious political debate.
"Of all our presidents he deserves reelection," said political analyst Nelson Navarro.
"I'd be surprised if he resisted the temptation ... But it's like a striptease. When you take off the last veil it's all over. (In his case) it will come off much later," he added.
By most accounts, Ramos is the most succesful president since World War Two.

No other Philippine head of state has been able to step down from office with their image intact except for the charismatic Ramon Magsaysay, also a former Defence Secretary, who died in a plane crash in 1957 while still in office.

Corazon Aquino's presidency before Ramos is remembered as largely ineffective, while the man she replaced -- Ferdinand Marcos -- is reviled for having brought the economy to its knees during his 20-year rule.

Businessmen make no bones of the fact they would like Ramos to stay on after next June when his term ends, so he can continue the reforms that have turned the country from the sick man of Asia to the next likely Asian tiger economy.
The barrier is the constitution. But the group which wants Ramos to run again claims to have 5.5 million signatures on their petition.
The Supreme Court has already banned the proposal and this week the Commission on Elections is due to give its verdict.
Ramos denies he has anything to do with it.
He also denies he plans to stand for a second term but -- and this is a fairly big "but" for many -- he does admit it is hard to ignore what he calls "the clamour" for him to stay on.
Some fear the debate over whether should Ramos run for president again will divide the country, just when its 70 million mostly poor population is beginning to have a real chance of prosperity.
The influential clergyman Cardinal Jaime Sin last week launched a fierce attack on what he described as proposals to "tinker" with the constitution.
"The proposed changes to the constitution are likely to harm the common good and the national interest," he said, arguing that Ramos had in any case failed to better the lot of the masses.

Many worry that changing the constitution for the sake of one individual could erode the hard-won democracy of the Philippines, which some of its more autocratic neighbours say could lead the country back into economic chaos.
But analysts say Manila's growing economic success is proof democracy can work and that tight political controls, which Singapore and Indonesia contend is a key to a booming economy, are not needed.
"The Philippines is beginning to offer an alternative model to that approach," British ambassador Adrian Thorpe said.
The gap between the rich and the poor is a constant theme in the run-up to the election, which is already lively although still 11 months away.
Most of the candidates have stressed the importance of spreading the wealth that has come with some of the most sustained economic growth the Philippines has ever seen.

Alex Magno, political scientist at the University of the Philippines, doubted Ramos would stay because the political cost would be too great and said he would instead pick a successor to continue his policies.
But for the moment, rather than become a lame-duck as the end of his term approaches, it is better to keep everyone guessing.
Magno said the current scramble among a dozen or so presidential hopefuls would fizzle out in a few months when most of their money was spent.
"The heavy artillery has not yet been put into place," he said.
The collapse of support for vice-president Joseph Estrada -- a former action film star with huge popularity among the masses -- was crucial, he said. After that, Ramos can pick his successor.
Perhaps Ramos's wife has the true answer.
"I have started packing up," Amelita Ramos told reporters recently.
